query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated first‐principles electron–phonon transport framework that explicitly and separately computes the phonon (lattice) and electron scattering contributions—including the influence of minor oxygen impurities—will predict thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr with roughly a 30% improvement in quantitative accuracy over previous conflated models, accurately matching independently measured lattice and electronic contributions at low (<200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy with equiatomic composition, typically modeled as a defect‐free crystal but with a minor (≈1 wt.%) oxygen impurity level, representing realistic processing conditions.
generation.intervention: Apply a computational framework that integrates first-principles calculations to separately determine phonon dispersion and anharmonic scattering as well as electron scattering mechanisms, explicitly incorporating the effect of oxygen impurities.
generation.conditions: The model will be evaluated over a temperature range from below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) up to 1200 K (reflecting high-temperature measurements on oxygen-containing specimens).
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale lattice dynamics (including vibrational anharmonicity and impurity-induced local distortions) that modulate phonon transport, coupled with electron scattering processes driven by alloy disorder and oxygen impurities.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling the thermal transport channels, the framework avoids oversimplifications (such as using a single Debye temperature) and calculates temperature-dependent contributions individually. This decoupling allows improved prediction of the total thermal conductivity by accurately capturing the independent behavior of phonons and electrons in a chemically complex, oxygen-doped environment.
generation.predicted_outcome: The separate predictions of lattice and electronic thermal conductivities will combine to yield a total conductivity that tracks experimental measurements within ±30% error, improving upon prior models by at least 30% in matching conductivity trends over the examined temperature range.
generation.baseline: Earlier computational approaches that assumed perfect, defect-free crystals and conflated phonon and electron contributions—often relying on debatable parameters like the Debye temperature—leading to less accurate predictions.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid primarily within the temperature range of <200 K to 1200 K and for samples with low-level oxygen impurities (~1 wt.%); its accuracy may diminish outside this regime or in samples with substantially different impurity profiles.
generation.uncertainty: While the model is anticipated to yield around a 30% improvement based on computational integration of electron–phonon interactions, uncertainties remain in quantifying the exact magnitude of improvement due to potential variations in impurity distributions and electron–phonon coupling strengths.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity. Use techniques (e.g., Raman or inelastic neutron scattering for phonon analysis and electrical resistivity measurements combined with the Wiedemann-Franz law for electronic conductivity) to independently measure the lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity over a temperature range from 100 K to 1300 K.
measurements: Lattice thermal conductivity from phonon spectrum analysis
Electronic thermal conductivity derived from electrical transport measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated framework fails to separately predict the lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity within an overall error margin better than ±30% relative to experimental measurements over the specified temperature range, or if the predicted decoupling of contributions is inconsistent with the independently measured values, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. The response of atoms to cluster or order in alloys offers deep insights to the microstructural behavior. This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. In Al x CrCoFeNi, the Al content can influence the final structural configuration [6] [23] [24] [25] [26] [27] due to the larger atom size, compared to other constituents, which considerably changes the lattice ordering. Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Over the past decade, models addressing thermal transport in refractory high-entropy alloys have taken incremental steps: early work varied atomic masses and force constants to modify lattice dynamics, later studies employed temperature‐dependent lattice transport models and even coupled DFT‐derived elastic properties with analytical conductivity estimates that rely on parameters like Debye temperatures. These approaches almost universally assumed ideal, defect‐free bulk crystals, so they conflated lattice phonon and electronic contributions—especially problematic for HfNbTaTiZr where experiments indicate both contributions can be significant. This trend has shown some ability to capture overall temperature dependence, but has not achieved a separable, quantitative prediction for the distinct channels.
decision.unsolved: The unsolved challenge is to predict, in a physically separating manner, the lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity for HfNbTaTiZr, particularly under realistic conditions (including minor oxygen impurities). Existing models do not capture the full atomic‐scale complexity and instead mix these contributions, leaving a gap in formulating a testable, predictive hypothesis that is applicable from low (<200 K) to high (up to 1200 K) temperatures.
decision.lever: an integrated first‐principles based electron–phonon transport framework that explicitly computes and decouples lattice vibrations from electronic scattering mechanisms, including the effect of minor oxygen impurities
decision.why: This approach logically follows from the limitations of prior work—by circumventing oversimplified parameters (e.g., Debye temperature) and the assumption of defect‐free crystals, it enables separate predictions for phonon and electron contributions. Expected improvements include at least a 30% better quantitative correspondence with measured total conductivity values, and applicability across the temperature ranges where, for instance, below 200 K the contributions are comparable while high‐temperature measurements (300–1200 K) provide stringent benchmarks. Decisive falsification would come from inability to match independent low-temperature electron and phonon conductivities, or a failure to predict the total conductivity trends observed in oxygen-containing specimens at high temperatures.
